Present tense of "вставать", used for a daily habit. Russian has no separate continuous form, so "я встаю" covers both "I get up" and "I am getting up". The pronoun "я" could be dropped, because the ending "-ю" already means "I".
Clock time takes "в" plus the number: "в семь", "в восемь". The word for o'clock, "часов", can be left out and usually is.
"Каждое" agrees with "утро", which is neuter, so it ends in "-ое". With a masculine noun you would say "каждый день", with a feminine one "каждую неделю". No preposition is used at all.
"Потом" means "then, after that". Russian would let you drop "я" here, since the ending of "делаю" already says who acts, but keeping it is never wrong.
An indeclinable masculine noun: "кофе" looks the same in every case, including the direct object. There is no article to add and no plural in this meaning.
The subject is not repeated after "и": one "я" covers both verbs, exactly as in English. "Новости" exists only in the plural, so anything agreeing with it must be plural too.
"Мой" agrees with the masculine noun "офис". With a feminine noun it becomes "моя", with a neuter one "моё". Russian has no articles, so the possessive is the only determiner here.

"Находится" literally means "is located". Russian normally drops the verb "to be" in the present tense, but for location this verb is the natural choice. "Рядом" means "nearby" and needs "с" to say what it is near.
The preposition "с" takes the instrumental case here: "вокзал" becomes "вокзалом". That ending is what marks the word's role — Russian uses endings where English uses word order.
"Идти" is the verb for going on foot, and specifically for one trip: now, or regularly in a described routine. Going by vehicle would be "ехать".
"Туда" already means "to there" — the direction is inside the word, so no preposition is added. "Там" would mean "there" with no movement.
"Пешком" means "on foot". Duration goes in the accusative with no preposition at all: "десять минут", not "в десять минут".
Negation is simply "не" placed right before the verb; there is no auxiliary like English "don't". The verb keeps its normal form: "не люблю".
"Любить" takes a direct object in the accusative, so both words change: "холодная погода" becomes "холодную погоду". Feminine nouns take "-у" and their adjectives take "-ую".
"Поэтому" means "that is why". "Дома" is a fixed adverb meaning "at home" — no preposition, and note it is stressed on the first syllable, unlike the plural of "дом".
"Сегодня" means "today". It is an adverb, takes no preposition and no article, and usually opens the sentence.
Russian says "на улице", literally "on the street", where English says "outside" or hides it inside the weather "it". The preposition "на" takes the prepositional case: "улица" becomes "улице".

Russian describes weather with a noun plus an adjective — literally "a strong wind". "Сильный" is masculine because "ветер" is, and the verb "is" is simply left out: the present tense of "быть" is not used in Russian.
"Мой" again, matching the masculine "брат". Family words behave like any other noun and take ordinary case endings.
Third person singular of "работать": "я работаю", "ты работаешь", "он работает". The ending carries the person, which is why the pronoun can be dropped.
"В" for location takes the prepositional case: "отель" becomes "в отеле", and the adjective follows suit, "большой" to "большом".
"Он" replaces "мой брат". The ending "-ет" marks third person singular and matches that pronoun.
Direct object in the accusative: "работа" becomes "работу". Feminine nouns ending in "-а" take "-у" there.
Clock time with "в", the same pattern as "в семь" in the first phrase.
This is how Russian says "we have": literally "at us there is". The owner follows "у" in the genitive, "мы" becoming "нас", and the thing owned is the grammatical subject.
Because "собака" is the subject, it stays in the nominative. It is feminine, so the adjective is "маленькая".
"Она" refers back to "собака", which is grammatically feminine — Russian follows the gender of the word even for a male dog. "Много" goes before the verb.
The instrumental case with no preposition expresses a regular time of day: "утром", "днём", "вечером", "ночью". One word does the work of English "in the evening".
"Гулять" means to walk for pleasure, not to walk somewhere. The ending "-ем" marks "мы".
"В" plus the prepositional case for being inside something: "парк" becomes "в парке".
Russian has no present-tense verb "to be", so "Я студент" is a complete sentence with no verb at all. Adding anything for "am" is the classic English-speaker mistake.
The noun stays in the nominative because it renames the subject. And there is no article: "a student" is simply "студент".
"Учу" comes from "учить", to study a subject. Language names are lower case in Russian: "испанский", never with a capital letter.
"Занятия" is plural, so the possessive is "мои". Russian prefers the plural here where English says "my class".
"Проходить" means "to take place". The ending "-ят" is third person plural, agreeing with the plural "занятия".
Days of the week take "в" plus the accusative: "в понедельник", "в четверг". The preposition is said once and covers both days.
"Этот" means "this", masculine to match "магазин". It becomes "эта" with feminine nouns and "это" with neuter ones.
A short-form adjective used as a predicate: "открыт" for masculine, "открыта" for feminine, "открыто" for neuter. No verb for "is" is needed.
"Каждый" is masculine because "день" is. Time expressions like this take the accusative, which for "день" happens to look like the nominative.
"Покупать" is the imperfective verb: it describes a repeated action, which is what "каждый день" requires. The perfective "куплю" would mean one single purchase.
Both "хлеб" and "молоко" are direct objects in the accusative, but neither changes shape: inanimate masculine and neuter nouns look the same in the nominative and the accusative.
"Здесь" means "here", with no preposition. "Сюда" would mean "to here" and is used with verbs of motion.
Masculine "телефон" takes "мой". Note that the possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.
"Очень" goes before the adjective. "Старый" is masculine to match "телефон", and again there is no word for "is".
"Он" replaces "телефон" — Russian pronouns follow grammatical gender, so an object can be "он" or "она". "Медленный" agrees with it in the masculine.
"Хотеть" is irregular: "я хочу", "ты хочешь", "он хочет". It is worth learning as a whole rather than by rule.
The adjective stands on its own and means "a new one" — Russian needs no equivalent of English "one". It is masculine because the implied noun is "телефон".
"В" plus the prepositional case for a period of time: "следующий год" becomes "в следующем году". Both words change their endings.
Days of the week take "в" plus the accusative: "суббота" becomes "в субботу".
"Убирать" is the imperfective, used because this happens every Saturday. The ending "-аю" marks "я".
"Свой" means "one's own" and always refers back to the subject; "мою" would be understood, but "свою" is what Russians say. Both words are accusative feminine: "своя комната" becomes "свою комнату".
"После" always takes the genitive, so "это" becomes "этого". The whole phrase means "after that".
"Готовить" means "to cook". Note the letter "л" that appears only in the first person: "готовлю", but "он готовит".
"Обед" is the direct object in the accusative and does not change form. "Для" always takes the genitive: "семья" becomes "семьи".
"Не" goes directly before the verb. "Пить" is irregular in the present: "я пью", "ты пьёшь", "они пьют".
Indeclinable, so the accusative object looks exactly like the dictionary form: "кофе". No article and no ending to add.
The instrumental with no preposition for a time of day, the same pattern as "утром" and "ночью".
"Это" means "this", referring to the whole previous idea. "Вредно" is a neuter short form used impersonally — there is no subject and no verb.
"Для" takes the genitive, so both words change: "мой сон" becomes "моего сна". Note that "сон" loses its vowel when it takes an ending.
"Поэтому" introduces the result. "Чай" is a masculine inanimate noun, so its accusative looks like the nominative.
